title: Gerontological and Palliative Care Nursing
description: Ageing and care of older adults, common geriatric syndromes, chronic disease and home-based care, palliative care, pain and symptom management, and end-of-life care in Nigeria.

topics.title: Ageing and Care of Older Adults
topics.summary: Demography, physiological changes of ageing, comprehensive assessment and care settings.

notes.b: Older persons (commonly ≥ 60 years in Africa) are a growing population in Nigeria; traditionally cared for by extended families, but urbanisation, migration and economic pressures are weakening family support, and formal geriatric services are limited (few geriatric centres, e.g. Chief Tony Anenih Geriatric Centre, UCH Ibadan). The National Senior Citizens Centre Act (2017) created a centre to address older people's needs. Physiological changes: reduced cardiac reserve, stiffer arteries (systolic hypertension), reduced lung elasticity, decreased renal function (lower GFR — affects drug clearance), reduced muscle mass (sarcopenia) and bone density, slower gastrointestinal motility, sensory decline (presbyopia, cataract, presbycusis), thinner skin, altered thermoregulation, reduced immunity, and changes in sleep. Normal ageing must be distinguished from disease (e.g. dementia and depression are not normal ageing). Ageism — negative stereotypes — affects care.

Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is a multidimensional, interdisciplinary evaluation of medical, functional (activities of daily living — Katz ADL: bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding; instrumental ADLs — Lawton: shopping, cooking, managing money and medicines), cognitive (MMSE, Mini-Cog), psychological (Geriatric Depression Scale), nutritional (Mini Nutritional Assessment), social and environmental domains, leading to a coordinated care plan. It improves outcomes and helps older people remain at home. Principles of gerontological nursing: promote independence and dignity, person-centred care, involve family and carers, prevent complications (falls, pressure ulcers, malnutrition, dehydration), review medications, and advocate against elder abuse (physical, psychological, financial, neglect).

topics.title: Geriatric Syndromes
topics.summary: Falls, frailty, delirium, dementia care, incontinence, polypharmacy and pressure ulcers.

notes.b: Geriatric syndromes are common, multifactorial conditions. Falls: risk factors — muscle weakness, gait and balance problems, poor vision, postural hypotension, cognitive impairment, incontinence, medications (sedatives, antihypertensives), footwear and environmental hazards (poor lighting, slippery floors, uneven surfaces, pit latrines); consequences — fractures (hip), fear of falling, loss of independence. Prevention: multifactorial risk assessment, strength and balance exercise, medication review, vision correction, home modifications (lighting, grab rails, clearing clutter), appropriate footwear and hip protectors. Frailty: a state of reduced physiological reserve (weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking, low activity — Fried phenotype) increasing vulnerability to stressors. Delirium: acute confusion with fluctuating attention — often the only sign of infection, dehydration, urinary retention, constipation or drug toxicity in older people; hypoactive delirium is easily missed; manage the cause, reorient, involve family, avoid restraints.
k: Delirium may be the only sign of illness

notes.b: Dementia care: person-centred approaches, maintain routine, clear simple communication, safe environment (wandering), manage behavioural and psychological symptoms (identify triggers — pain, hunger, infection — before medicating; antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk), support carers (burden and stress), advance care planning while capacity remains; stigma and beliefs about witchcraft can lead to abuse of people with dementia in some communities. Urinary incontinence (stress, urge, overflow, functional): assess causes (UTI, constipation, drugs — diuretics, prostate enlargement), bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, scheduled toileting, skin care; catheters as a last resort (infection risk). Polypharmacy (≥ 5 medicines) increases adverse drug reactions, interactions, falls and non-adherence — regular medication review and deprescribing (Beers criteria, STOPP/START). Pressure ulcers: risk assessment (Braden/Waterlow), repositioning, support surfaces, nutrition and continence care; staging (1 — non-blanching erythema, which may appear darker/purplish in dark skin — to 4 — full thickness with bone, muscle or tendon exposed).
k: Pressure ulcer stages; dark skin signs

topics.title: Chronic Disease and Home-Based Care
topics.summary: Managing chronic conditions in older adults, home-based and community care, and carer support.

notes.b: Older Nigerians commonly live with multiple chronic conditions (multimorbidity): hypertension, diabetes, osteoarthritis, stroke sequelae, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cataract and glaucoma, prostate disease, cancers, dementia and depression. Nursing roles: self-management education (medications, diet, exercise, recognising deterioration), monitoring (BP, glucose, weight), adherence support (pill boxes, simplified regimens, involving family), nutrition (risk of malnutrition and dehydration — reduced thirst sensation), exercise and mobility, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal where available), sensory aids (spectacles, hearing aids), foot care in diabetes, and coordination with other services. Financial barriers are major since most care is paid out-of-pocket; the NHIA and state schemes are beginning to cover older adults, and some states (e.g. Ekiti, Osun, Lagos) have social welfare or health programmes for older people.

Home-based care (HBC) provides care in the patient's home by nurses, community health workers and families — valuable for chronically ill, bedridden and dying patients, and widely used in HIV/AIDS programmes and palliative care. Components: assessment of home environment and needs, nursing procedures (wound care, catheter care, medication administration), teaching carers (positioning, lifting, feeding, hygiene, infection prevention), provision of supplies, referral, psychosocial and spiritual support, and bereavement support. Family carers often experience burden (physical, emotional, financial, social) and need information, training, respite and support groups. Community resources include faith-based organisations, NGOs, and community health extension workers. Nurses should assess carer strain and involve families in care planning while respecting the patient's autonomy and cultural values.

topics.title: Palliative Care Principles and Pain Management
topics.summary: Definition, models of palliative care, pain assessment, WHO analgesic ladder and opioids.

notes.b: WHO defines palliative care as an approach that improves the quality of life of patients (adults and children) and their families facing problems associated with life-threatening illness, through prevention and relief of suffering by early identification, impeccable assessment and treatment of pain and other problems — physical, psychosocial and spiritual ('total pain', Cicely Saunders). It affirms life, regards dying as a normal process, neither hastens nor postpones death, and offers a support system for families including bereavement. It is applicable early in illness alongside curative treatment. Common conditions: cancer (breast, cervical, prostate, liver), HIV/AIDS, end-stage organ failure, stroke, dementia and sickle cell disease. Nigeria has limited palliative services (hospital-based teams in teaching hospitals, few hospices — e.g. Hospice and Palliative Care Association of Nigeria), with most patients dying at home; integrating palliative care into primary care and nursing roles is a priority. The interdisciplinary team includes nurses, doctors, social workers, chaplains/imams, pharmacists and volunteers.
k: Total pain: physical, psychological, social, spiritual

notes.b: Pain is whatever the patient says it is. Assess using PQRST (provoking factors, quality, region/radiation, severity — numeric rating or faces scales, timing), plus effect on function and mood; reassess regularly. The WHO analgesic approach: 'by mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual, with attention to detail' — non-opioids (paracetamol, NSAIDs) ± adjuvants, weak opioids (codeine, tramadol) or low-dose strong opioids, then strong opioids (oral morphine — the gold standard). Regular (around-the-clock) dosing with breakthrough doses (about one-sixth of the total daily dose). Always prescribe a laxative with opioids; manage nausea; monitor for sedation and respiratory depression (rare with careful titration). Adjuvants: amitriptyline or gabapentin (neuropathic pain), steroids (bone pain, raised ICP, nerve compression), NSAIDs (bone pain), and radiotherapy. Barriers in Nigeria: limited availability of oral morphine (NAFDAC and hospitals now produce oral morphine solution), fears of addiction among patients and health workers (opiophobia), and restrictive regulations. Non-drug measures: positioning, massage, heat/cold, relaxation, music and spiritual support.
k: Pain is what the patient says

topics.title: Symptom Control and End-of-Life Care
topics.summary: Managing breathlessness, nausea and other symptoms, care in the last days, and bereavement.

notes.b: Common symptoms and nursing management: breathlessness (sit upright, fan to the face, calm environment, oxygen if hypoxic, low-dose oral morphine, treat causes — effusion, anaemia, infection), nausea and vomiting (identify cause — drugs, constipation, bowel obstruction, raised ICP, hypercalcaemia; antiemetics — metoclopramide, haloperidol, cyclizine, ondansetron; small frequent meals), constipation (prevention with laxatives, fluids, mobility), anorexia and cachexia (small appetising meals, relieve mouth problems, avoid force-feeding), mouth care (thrush — antifungals; dry mouth — frequent sips, lip balm), fatigue, fungating wounds (odour control with metronidazole, charcoal dressings; bleeding control), lymphoedema, anxiety and depression, and spiritual distress. Nurses coordinate care, involve patients in decisions and respect their preferred place of care and death.

Recognising dying: increasing weakness and sleepiness, reduced intake, difficulty swallowing, changes in breathing (Cheyne–Stokes, noisy 'death rattle' secretions), cool mottled peripheries and reduced urine output. Care in the last days: review and stop non-essential medicines and observations, ensure anticipatory medicines are available (for pain, breathlessness, agitation, nausea and secretions — e.g. morphine, midazolam, haloperidol, hyoscine butylbromide), mouth care, positioning, pressure area care, continence care, and emotional and spiritual support for the patient and family; honour religious and cultural rites (e.g. prayers, presence of religious leaders, Muslim burial within 24 hours, Christian last rites). Communicate honestly and compassionately (the SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions/Empathy, Strategy/Summary). After death: last offices with dignity according to cultural and religious practice, certification, and support for the family. Grief (Kübler-Ross stages — denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance — not strictly linear) and bereavement support; complicated grief may need referral. Nurses also need support to prevent burnout and compassion fatigue.
